concept.title: Choosing the Right Wi-Fi Band (2.4 GHz vs 5 GHz)
concept.shortdesc: The 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz Wi-Fi bands provide different coverage, performance, and device compatibility. Select a band based on the device location, network requirements, and wireless environment.

section.title: Overview
section.p: The supports . The router can use the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz frequency bands to communicate with wireless devices.

The 2.4 GHz band usually provides more coverage and better signal transmission through physical obstructions. The 5 GHz band usually provides higher data rates and experiences less interference from nearby devices.
section.note: Use 2.4 GHz when a device is far from the router. Use 5 GHz when a compatible device is near the router and requires increased network performance.
The actual performance of each band depends on signal strength, channel utilization, channel width, client capabilities, physical obstructions, and nearby wireless networks.

section.title: 2.4 GHz Band
section.p: The 2.4 GHz band provides wireless coverage over a larger area than the 5 GHz band. Its signal can usually pass through walls and floors more effectively.
Many older wireless devices and IoT devices support the 2.4 GHz band. This band is suitable for devices that require more coverage and do not require high data rates.
The 2.4 GHz band is suitable for:

ul.li: Devices that are far from the router
Devices separated from the router by walls or floors
Devices that send small amounts of data

section.note: The 2.4 GHz band can experience interference from nearby Wi-Fi networks, microwave ovens, Bluetooth devices, cordless telephones, and other wireless equipment.

The 2.4 GHz band has limited non-overlapping channel capacity. Avoid channel overlap when you manually configure the wireless channel. Available channels and permitted channel usage depend on regional regulations.

section.title: 5 GHz Band
section.p: The 5 GHz band usually provides higher data rates than the 2.4 GHz band. It also provides more channel options and can experience less interference in many wireless environments.
The 5 GHz signal has a shorter coverage range and is more affected by walls, floors, and other physical obstructions. Use this band for compatible devices that are near the .
The 5 GHz band is suitable for:

ul.li: Devices that are near the router
Devices that require higher network throughput

section.note: If a device loses its connection on 5 GHz, connect the device to the 2.4 GHz band and test the connection again.
The default advanced configuration in this guide uses with on the . Confirm that this configuration is permitted in the applicable regulatory region and suitable for the local wireless environment.

IoT devices, basic network use, and distant devices

section.title: Select a Wi-Fi Band
section.p: Select the 2.4 GHz band when coverage and device compatibility are more important than network speed.
Select the 5 GHz band when a compatible device is near the router and requires higher network performance.
Keep both bands enabled when possible. This configuration lets compatible client devices use the band that provides a suitable connection.
section.note: Do not select a band based only on its maximum supported data rate. Distance, obstructions, interference, and device capabilities can affect actual performance.

section.title: Device Band Recommendations

section.note: These recommendations are general guidelines. Test the connection on each device before you select the final band.

section.title: Automatic Band Selection
section.p: The can use one Wi-Fi network name for both frequency bands if automatic band selection is available. The router or client device can then select a suitable band.
Automatic band selection simplifies device connectivity because users do not have to select a separate network for each band.
section.note: Keep automatic band selection enabled unless a device has a connection problem.
Band-selection behavior depends on the access point and client device. A client device can remain connected to a band even when another band can provide better performance.

section.title: Separate Network Names
section.p: Separate network names let users select a specific frequency band. This configuration can help identify a band-related connection problem.
Use separate network names only when you must control the band that a client device uses. Keep one network name when automatic band selection provides reliable operation.
section.note: Separate SSIDs can simplify controlled testing and device placement. However, they can prevent automatic movement between bands and can increase network management requirements.

section.title: Evaluate the Selected Band
section.p: Test the connection in the location where the client device is normally used.
Check the signal strength, connection stability, and network performance. Test the other band if the connection is slow or unstable.
section.note: Move the device closer to the router and test the connection again. If the connection improves, distance or an obstruction can be the cause of the problem.
Compare signal strength, channel utilization, throughput, latency, and packet loss on both bands. Use the same client device, test location, and network activity for each test.
